Chapter 1. How Body Shame Begins and Why It Persists.
Think back for a moment—can you remember the first time you felt out of place in your own skin? Maybe it was when you were a kid, sitting in class, realizing your body didn’t look like the ones in magazines, or maybe you picked up on those quiet comments from classmates. That feeling of discomfort... it didn’t come from inside you. It began with the way the world looked at you, with those unspoken rules that some bodies are just “better” than others.
This is where body shame often starts. Not because you did something wrong, but because family, media, and society quietly teach us that certain bodies are problems to be solved.
Picture this: at home, a parent sighs in front of the mirror, tugging at clothes that never seem to fit quite right. Their child watches, picking up on the message—that maybe bodies are something to be fixed. Or at school, friends compare how they look, everyone secretly measuring themselves, hoping for a little bit of approval. All these moments pile up, shaping the way we see ourselves, sometimes long before we even know how to talk about it.
Here’s something to pay attention to: most people don’t realize that body shame isn’t just part of being human. It’s learned—like a family recipe passed down through generations, and it’s everywhere. Ads, movies, even advice from people who mean well... they all reinforce this idea that only certain bodies deserve love, respect, or even basic dignity.
Look around: it’s in the way clothes are sized, the stories we hear about who gets to be the hero, and even in the awkward silence when someone who looks different walks into a room. For a lot of us, struggling with body image becomes a daily battle. Some try to shrink themselves, hoping to fade into the background, while others push to stand out—just trying to prove they matter. The pain is very real, but it’s not just about one person’s feelings. It’s built right into the fabric of our society, touching everything from healthcare and relationships to how we simply move through the world.
Then, there’s this moment—maybe in a doctor’s office, when you’re told your health issues are all because of your size, no real investigation. Or maybe it’s in a store, where nothing fits, and you can feel the sales clerk’s eyes linger a little too long. These aren’t just random experiences—they’re part of a much bigger pattern, one that devalues some bodies and puts others on a pedestal.
Here’s the hard truth: body shame actually serves a purpose for those in power. It keeps us distracted—so busy worrying about fixing ourselves, we forget to question the system that made us feel broken in the first place. When we’re wrapped up in appearance, we have less energy to challenge injustice or push for real change. That’s how body shame becomes a tool—a way to keep things just as they are.
But what if you could see things differently? Some people start to question those messages, asking themselves, “Who really benefits from my discomfort?” And that’s when something shifts. You realize the problem isn’t your body—it’s the world’s refusal to accept difference. This is the beginning of something bigger: a kind of love that doesn’t apologize for existing, a love that says every body deserves dignity and respect.
The journey away from body shame isn’t simple. It means unlearning years of conditioning, challenging beliefs you might not even know you have, and facing some hard truths. But it really is possible. And it all starts with this: your body is not the enemy. The real problem lies in the systems that taught you to hate yourself. And those systems? They can be changed.
